parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation
parent.overview: White plays 2.c3 to follow with d4 and get the ideal e4+d4 pawn centre without entering the heavily analysed Open Sicilian. Black's two real answers are 2...d5 (Barmen: 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4) and 2...Nf6 (3.e5 Nd5), with 2...e6 and 2...Nc6 as quieter routes that often transpose to French Advance or Maroczy-like structures. The game usually settles into structure play: an isolated d4 pawn for White after the Barmen exchanges, or an Alekhine-style space-versus-targets fight after 2...Nf6. Sources describe it as solid, theory-light and positional rather than tactical, giving White a small but reliable edge; it is far more common at club level than at the top, though Kasparov, Anand, Kramnik, Carlsen and Sveshnikov have all used it. Note: this brief covers the root 2.c3 only; the database's most-played branch is 2...Nc6 (3.Nf3 / 3.d4), which the sources barely discuss (s3 only says 2...Nc6 dominates at lower ratings). The same position appears as 'Sicilian: Alapin' in alternative names and should classify identically.

parent.name: English Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...b6 (or 1...e6 2.c4 b6) intending ...Bb7, a hypermodern set-up in which the bishop on b7 pressures e4 and the centre rather than occupying it. After 3.e4 Bb7 White builds a broad pawn centre (Bd3, f3, Nc3) and Black undermines it with ...Bb4(+), ...f5 and sometimes ...Qh4, as in Polugaevsky-Korchnoi 1977 (4.Qc2 Qh4 5.Nd2 Bb4). The play is double-edged: Black gives White space and a strong centre, then goes for counterplay and tactics against it. Gambit versions (Hartlaub 4...f5, Polli 4.f3 f5) and 3.Nc3 Bb4 transpositions to a ...b6 Nimzo-Indian are the main branches. It was a surprise weapon of Speelman, Short, Miles and Keene in the 1980s and is rare in elite play, although some club players use 1...b6/2...Bb7 as a universal system.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Symmetrical Variation
parent.overview: This is a crossroads reached by symmetrical knight development: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6. Nothing is committed in the centre; the character is decided by White's third move. 3.c4 transposes to Queen's Gambit structures (QGD, Slav, Semi-Slav, QGA) and is by far the most played continuation in the database; 3.g3 gives the Pseudo-Catalan (a Catalan-style fianchetto); 3.e3 with Bd3 and c3 is the Colle; 3.Bf4 or 2.Bf4 is the London; 3.c3 is a flexible quiet set-up. Wikipedia and ChessBase describe the non-c4 lines as closed-centre system play with simple development plans and little theory. Black is generally free to develop logically (...e6, ...c5 or ...c6, ...Bf5/Bg4).

root.name: Old Indian Defense: Aged Gibbon Gambit

parent.name: Old Indian Defense
parent.overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.
